findings.title: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of ||, breaking the permission check
findings.body: The check is `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`, but the variable is named and intended as 'admin OR owner'. With the AND, a user who is a team admin but not the team owner is denied (FORBIDDEN), and a team owner who is not recorded as an admin is also denied. The intended behavior (matching other handlers in the codebase, e.g. editLocation, which use `||`) is that either role grants permission. Consequence: team admins cannot add guests to team bookings even though the UI/API contract suggests they should be able to.

findings.title: Guest emails are not deduplicated against each other, only against existing attendees
findings.body: The server-side Zod schema (addGuests.schema.ts) only validates that each string is an email; the uniqueness refinement exists only in the client-side dialog. The handler's `uniqueGuests` filter only removes guests that already exist in `booking.attendees` or are blacklisted — it never dedupes the request array itself. A request like `{ bookingId, guests: ["a@b.com", "a@b.com"] }` passes validation and the subsequent `createMany` inserts two identical attendee rows for the same booking, corrupting the attendee list and causing duplicate emails/ICS invites. The uniqueness constraint must be enforced server-side (in the schema or by deduping `uniqueGuests`).

findings.title: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS check is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: The blacklist is normalized with `.toLowerCase()` (`process.env.BLACKLISTED_GUEST_emails.split(",").map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`), but the incoming `guest` values are compared without normalization: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. An email like `Bad@Example.com` will not match a blacklisted `bad@example.com` and will be added, defeating the blacklist. The same case-sensitivity problem affects `guest === attendee.email` on line 76 and the `isAttendee` check on line 52 (`attendee.email === user.email`), allowing duplicate attendee entries that differ only in case. All email comparisons here should be case-insensitive.

findings.title: EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials, not the booking organizer's
findings.body: The handler authorizes team admins/owners and attendees (not just the organizer) to add guests, but then constructs `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` using `ctx.user` (the caller) and credentials from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. When a team owner or an attendee triggers this mutation, the calendar update (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) runs with the wrong user's calendar credentials — most likely none matching the booking's destination calendar — so the external calendar event is not updated for the new guests, or the operation errors. The EventManager should be constructed from the booking organizer (`booking.user`, which is already included with credentials in the initial query) so calendar attendee updates work regardless of who calls the endpoint.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores disableStandardEmails event type metadata
findings.body: Every other email-sending function in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendRescheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, etc.) accepts an `eventTypeMetadata` parameter and skips host/attendee emails when `disableStandardEmails.all.host` / `.attendee` is set. The new `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata and unconditionally sends both organizer and attendee emails. Event types that have standard emails disabled (a supported configuration) will still blast out 'Guests Added' emails to hosts and attendees, violating the organizer's email preferences. The function should accept and honor `eventTypeMetadata` like its siblings.

findings.title: No booking status or seat-capacity checks before adding guests
findings.body: The handler never checks `booking.status`, so guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings; those guests then receive an email with an ICS of `status: "CONFIRMED"` (attendee-add-guests-email.ts line 15) for an event that no longer exists. Additionally, for event types with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, the handler blindly `createMany`s attendees with no capacity check and without creating the associated `seatsReferences`/booking-seat records that the seats flow relies on, which can overbook a seat-limited event and leave attendee records in a state that breaks seat cancellation logic.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails is called with the raw `guests` input instead of the guests actually added
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original request array, but only `uniqueGuests` were actually persisted. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` decides whether an attendee gets the 'scheduled' email (as a new guest) or the 'guests added' notification. If a requested email was filtered out (already an attendee with different casing, or blacklisted), the classification is made against emails that were never added, and emails that *were* added are classified using stale input. Passing `uniqueGuests` (normalized to match stored attendee emails) would make the recipient classification accurate.

findings.title: Email send failure is silently swallowed with console.log
findings.body: The catch block is `catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` — the caught `err` is discarded, no logger is used, and the mutation still returns success ("Guests added"). Operators get no signal (no structured log, no error) when guest notification emails fail, making delivery problems undiagnosable. At minimum log the error via the `logger` used elsewhere in the codebase and include the booking id.

findings.title: Hardcoded, untranslated user-facing string "Remove email"
findings.body: The tooltip content in the MultiEmail component is the literal string `"Remove email"` while every other user-facing string in the new components goes through `t()` / `useLocale()`. Non-English users will see English text for this tooltip. It should use `t("remove_email")` (with the key added to common.json), consistent with the rest of the file.

findings.title: Error toast renders raw TRPC error codes and the fallback message is unreachable
findings.body: `const message = \`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}\`` produces strings like "BAD_REQUEST: emails_must_be_unique_valid" or "undefined: ..." when `err.data` is missing, exposing internal error codes to users. Additionally, `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` never falls back because a template literal is always truthy, so the newly added "unable_to_add_guests" locale string is dead code. Errors that aren't translation keys (e.g. network failures) will also be passed to `t()` verbatim. The message should be mapped from known error codes to translated, human-readable text.
